answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type (cluster): Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (resource name example: myCluster).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: CLI group: az documentdb mongodb or az documentdb mongo (core CLI group under the Microsoft.DocumentDB provider). Example command to create: az documentdb mongo cluster create --name myCluster --resource-group myRg --location eastus --sku M30 --replica-count 3. This is provided in the core 'az documentdb' command group (not a 3rd-party extension).

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: resource type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters@2024-01-01' (example snippet: resource mongoCluster 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters@2024-01-01' = { name: 'myCluster' location: 'eastus' properties: { sku: { name: 'M30' } } }). Terraform (AzureRM): use azurerm_resource 'azurerm_documentdb_mongo_cluster' (provider resource name: azurerm_documentdb_mongo_cluster) or, if using generic ARM via azurerm_resource, type = "Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters" with appropriate api_version and properties.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical connection string example: mongodb://username:password@mycluster.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Scheme: mongodb:// (or mongodb+srv:// if SRV is supported). Host suffix: .mongo.cosmos.azure.com. TLS port: 10255. Required options: ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false. Use the account's primary user and key (or user-scoped password) as the credentials.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is billed by compute-tier (vCore-like instance tiers such as M30, M50, etc) and storage; clusters are sized with named SKUs (e.g. M30) and charged per vCore/VM equivalent plus storage. Some SKUs or regions may offer serverless or autoscale options, but primary billing model for a DocumentDB Mongo cluster is compute-tier (vCore/instance) + storage.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Primary supported method for MongoDB drivers: SCRAM username/password (MongoDB users created on the cluster). X.509 client certificate authentication is supported in some SKUs. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) is not directly supported as a MongoDB driver auth mechanism; management operations can use Azure AD for ARM/API calls, but the MongoDB wire protocol client must use SCRAM credentials or client certs. (If AAD integration exists, driver obtains an AAD token and the service exchanges it server-side — but that is not a standard MongoDB driver flow.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the official MongoDB drivers (for Node.js use the 'mongodb' npm package, e.g. const { MongoClient } = require('mongodb')). There is no separate service-specific MongoDB driver; do not use @azure/cosmos for MongoDB workloads. Management tasks (creating clusters) use Azure CLI/ARM/Bicep/Terraform or Azure management SDKs, but application data access uses standard MongoDB drivers.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Supported index types (cluster in the sample): HNSW, IVF and DiskANN for knn (vector) indexes. Example MongoDB createIndex syntax (MongoDB 7-style knn vector index): db.providers.createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, { knnVector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', dimensions: 1536, 'searchRuntimeOptions': {} } }); Replace algorithm with 'ivf' or 'diskann' and include algorithm-specific options (e.g. efConstruction for hnsw).

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: For basic text search use MongoDB text indexes: db.collection.createIndex({ description: 'text', notes: 'text' }). For hybrid vector+text (semantic + vector) searches, use a two-step approach: 1) run a kNN vector search using the vector index to retrieve nearest candidates (aggregate with $knnSearch or a vector score stage depending on engine), 2) re-rank/filter those candidates by text matching or combine scores in application logic. There is no separate Azure Search integration invoked from the MongoDB wire protocol; if you need Azure Cognitive Search you must index data into Azure Search separately.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: The cluster in the sample supports MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol and MongoDB 7-compatible features (including 7.0 vector index support). Common caveats: server-side JS or certain low-level admin commands may be restricted; some storage-engine-specific features and internal commands (e.g. full admin access to replica-set control) are not exposed. Multi-document transactions and change streams are supported in modern clusters, but their behaviour/latency may differ from unmanaged MongoDB. (Expect some management-level features to be restricted.)

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no Microsoft-provided local emulator that perfectly matches the managed DocumentDB MongoDB service. For local development use the official MongoDB server Docker image (e.g. mongo:7.0) or a local MongoDB install. Default MongoDB port: 27017. Use a local docker run --name local-mongo -p 27017:27017 -d mongo:7.0.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Yes — change streams are supported on modern MongoDB-compatible clusters (MongoDB 7.0). No special Azure management toggle is required for basic change streams; application code uses collection.watch() or client.watch(). If you need cross-region or longer retention guarantees, ensure the cluster is provisioned with replication and sufficient oplog/history retention via cluster sizing.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server profile (the documentdb MCP server) to run data-plane inspection tools for the managed DocumentDB Mongo clusters. The general Azure MCP server (for generic ARM/management) will not expose Mongo-specific inspection helpers; the documentdb MCP server is the service-specific one to use.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically 'DocumentDB' referred to Microsoft's earlier NoSQL service that evolved into Azure Cosmos DB (the name changed years ago). The new managed MongoDB-compatible offering is sometimes referred to in docs as the DocumentDB Mongo service or 'Azure DocumentDB (Mongo)'. Relation: this service is Microsoft-managed MongoDB-compatible hosting (not the open-source 'DocumentDB' project); it is distinct from the Azure Cosmos DB SQL/Core API (which uses RU-based model). It is a separate managed MongoDB-compatible product rather than the original Cosmos DB SQL API.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underlying engine: a MongoDB-compatible server implementation (built from upstream MongoDB binaries/enterprise or Microsoft-managed fork) that speaks the MongoDB wire protocol. Effect on app code: minimal — use standard MongoDB drivers and query language. Some admin or edge features may differ and certain server-level ops may be restricted, but normal CRUD, aggregation, indexes (including knn vector indexes on supported versions) and transactions work the same.

answers.question: What exact connection code and options will the sample use to connect from Node.js to the cluster (reading DOCUMENTDB_URI from env)?
answers.answer: Node.js connection: use the 'mongodb' driver. Example code: const { MongoClient } = require('mongodb'); const uri = process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI; const client = new MongoClient(uri, { tls: true, tlsInsecure: false, useUnifiedTopology: true }); await client.connect(); (Expect the URI to include host:port and ?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false or use mongodb+srv URI if provided.)

answers.question: Which database name and collections will the sample create and use?
answers.answer: Use database name 'sample_healthcare_05'. Collections: 'providers' (provider documents with availabilitySlots and optional embedding vectors), 'appointments' (appointment documents storing patient, providerId, slot info, status), and 'patients' (optional patient profiles).

answers.question: What index definitions does this sample need (including vector index syntax) so availability vector search, slot lookup and atomic updates are efficient?
answers.answer: Indexes to create at startup: 1) Vector index on provider availability embeddings: db.providers.createIndex({ availabilityEmbedding: 'knnVector' }, { knnVector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', dimensions: 1536 } }) 2) Appointment unique key on provider+slot time: db.appointments.createIndex({ providerId: 1, slotStart: 1 }, { unique: true }) 3) Query indexes: db.providers.createIndex({ providerId: 1 }), db.appointments.createIndex({ patientId: 1, status: 1 }).

answers.question: How will the sample perform atomic slot reservation and rescheduling (command example)?
answers.answer: Use a multi-document transaction or an atomic findOneAndUpdate with a conditional check. Example using transactions: const session = client.startSession(); await session.withTransaction(async () => { const prov = await providers.findOne({ _id: pid }, { session }); // check slot available await appointments.insertOne({ providerId: pid, slotStart, patientId, status: 'booked' }, { session }); await providers.updateOne({ _id: pid, 'slots.start': slotStart, 'slots.status': 'free' }, { $set: { 'slots.$.status': 'booked' } }, { session }); }); Alternatively use findOneAndUpdate on appointments with upsert:false and conditional query (providerId + slotStart + status:'free') and $set to acquire atomically.

answers.question: Does the sample rely on change streams for agent memory or conversation sync, and how will it subscribe?
answers.answer: Yes: the agent will use change streams to observe appointment updates and to keep conversation memory in sync. Subscribe using the mongodb change stream API: const changeStream = appointments.watch([], { fullDocument: 'updateLookup' }); changeStream.on('change', change => { /* update in-memory agent memory or LangChain vector store */ }); Ensure the cluster supports change streams and the app has permission to watch the collection.
